RSR.board.title: Situation Room
RSR.board.noPlots: Nothing is stirring yet. The GM has not opened any Plots.
RSR.board.noThreads: No Threads are running on this Plot yet.
RSR.turn.tooltip:
The clock the whole board rides. Advancing it pays every Force its income, unless you have paused that Force, and moves every running condition timer.

A Plot that keeps its own Cycle sits this out and is advanced from its own button. The confirmation names any that will.
RSR.editor.name: Name
RSR.editor.deletePlotWarning: Delete "{name}" and its {count} Thread(s)? Any Asset committed to them is released, not deleted. This cannot be undone.
RSR.editor.stateHint: The bar needs a range to fill against. Minimum and maximum are yours to choose; State can be negative if that suits the Plot.
RSR.editor.phasesHint:
The ladder this Plot’s State climbs. One card per Phase: the State it begins at, its name, the colour it paints the bar, the line printed under the bar for everyone, and the notes that stay yours.

There is no reordering handle. Phases sort themselves by threshold when you save, so a card put in at the bottom finds its own place.

A Phase can also reveal a Thread you have locked, or lock one that was open. Both hold for as long as State stands at or above that Phase, and a later Phase overrules an earlier one about the same Thread — so State falling back reopens what the situation had closed.

Only the Phase a Plot is currently in is ever shown at the table — never the ones ahead of it.
RSR.editor.turnBehaviourHint:
Which clock this Plot keeps.

  • Default — moves with the Global Cycle.
  • Isolated — ignores it, and gets a button of its own: a journey counted in months can sit still while a siege counted in weeks moves.
  • None — keeps no clock at all, and has no button.

A Cycle moves this Plot’s own count and the timers on the Assets committed to it — never anybody’s income, which belongs to the Force.
RSR.editor.turnLabelHint:
What this Plot’s own clock is called wherever it is named: the chip beside the Plot’s name, the button that moves it, and the line it writes in Latest Developments.

Leave it empty for Plot Cycle. Only a Plot that keeps its own Cycle draws one at all — a Plot riding the Global Cycle never shows a clock of its own.
RSR.editor.defaultModeHint:
What new Threads on this Plot use unless they override it.

  • Narrative — tracks nothing; you conclude it by hand.
  • Investment — one shared pool.
  • Clock — segments you tick.
  • Contested — every Force its own pile, and it never concludes itself.
RSR.editor.deleteThreadWarning: Delete "{name}"? It is removed from every prerequisite list, and any Asset committed to it is released. This cannot be undone.
RSR.editor.thresholdHint: How much investment concludes this Thread. Used by Investment and Contested modes.
RSR.editor.segmentsHint: How many ticks fill the clock. Used by Clock mode only.
RSR.editor.outcomesHint: What this Plot's State does if that Force is the one who concludes this Thread. A row left at zero with no note is not recorded.
RSR.editor.noForcesOnPlot: This Plot has no Forces yet, so there is nothing to win it.
RSR.editor.prereqsHint:
This Thread stays shut until every Thread named here has concluded. It is a separate gate from the Locked status and from a Phase: a Phase that reveals this Thread does not pay off its requirements.

A Thread that already waits on this one is not offered, at any depth — two Threads waiting on each other would never open.

A player is never told the name of a requirement they cannot already see, only that there is one.
RSR.help.plots.title: Plots, State and Phases
RSR.help.plots.body.gm:
A Plot is one running situation — an invasion, an investigation, a fragile treaty. It carries a single number, its State, and the bands along that number are its Phases.

  • State is yours to define. Set the range in the Plot editor; it can run negative if that suits the fiction.
  • Phases relabel and recolour the chip beside the bar as State crosses each threshold. You write the label, the tone, and private notes for yourself.
  • A Phase can also reveal a Thread you have locked, or lock one that was open — both named on the Phase’s own card. See Gates and requirements.
  • Each Phase is a card in the Plot editor holding both of its texts: what the table sees, printed under the State bar for everyone, and your own notes, which stay yours. Cards sort themselves by threshold, so the ladder is always in order.
  • Groupings arrange the roster under headings you choose. They are cosmetic: nothing reads them, they just answer "whose side is who on" at a glance.
  • Lifecycle — Active, Paused, Resolved, Archived — decides whether the Plot is live on the board. Archived Plots leave the board entirely.
  • Cycle behaviour decides which clock this Plot keeps. Default moves with the Global Cycle, pressed above the Plot list. Isolated ignores it and gets a Plot Cycle of its own, with a button beside the Plot’s name — for the journey counted in months that should not move three days every time a siege counted in weeks does. None keeps no clock at all and has no button. A Plot that keeps its own can be given its own name for it: Days on the Road, Moons, whatever the fiction counts in. A Cycle moves that Plot’s own count and the timers on the Assets committed to it — never anybody’s income, which belongs to the Force.

The table only ever sees the label of the Phase the Plot is in right now, never the ones waiting further up the track. You can write Rain of Fire today without warning anyone it exists.
RSR.help.plots.body.player:
A Plot is one running situation your characters care about — an invasion, an investigation, a treaty that may not hold.

  • The bar is how far it has swung.
  • The word beside it names where things stand at the moment, and the line under it says what that looks like.
  • The Forces listed below are who is involved, arranged by the side they are on.

It is not a countdown to anything you have been told about. It describes now.
RSR.help.threads.title: Threads
RSR.help.threads.body.gm:
Threads are the moving parts of a Plot — the things being attempted inside it. Each fills toward its own threshold, and concluding one moves the Plot’s State.

  • A Thread belongs to the Plot, not to a Force, so two sides can push the same Thread in opposite directions.
  • Outcomes are written per Force: what State does if this side is the one who carries it.
  • Prerequisites hold a Thread shut until the ones it names conclude — one of three ways a Thread can be shut, and the only one the table is ever told the name of. See Gates and requirements.

A locked Thread never names a prerequisite the viewer cannot already see. A player is told something has to happen first, not what.
RSR.help.threads.body.player:
Threads are the moving parts of a Plot — the things being attempted inside it. Each has its own bar, and when one finishes it shifts the whole Plot, for better or worse depending on who got there.

Some Threads are waiting on others — the Requirements view beside this list draws which. Some you are only told exist.
RSR.help.state.title: What you are allowed to see
RSR.help.state.body.gm:
Every Plot, Thread, Force and Asset carries a visibility setting, plus a separate switch for whether its numbers show.

  • Visible — the table sees it.
  • Masked — the row appears, and reads as Unknown activity — ??? or whatever its kind of row calls itself. They know something is there and roughly what sort of something — and nothing else about it, including what kind of Thread it is.
  • Hidden — never drawn for them at all.
  • Hide values — visible, but without numbers. Use this when the table should know a Thread is running without knowing how close it is.
  • Called — what THIS row says while it is masked, if the default is not the right lie. Somebody is asking questions — ??? tells the table more than Unknown activity without telling them who.
  • Instead of the bar — a line the table reads in place of a masked Plot’s State bar, or a masked Thread’s own reading. Write one when they have heard about something rather than watched it: a bar says how far along it is, and a rumour is not that precise. Leave it empty and the bar stays, which is the usual case.
  • New rows start at whatever Campaign defaults says for their kind — Plots, Threads, Forces and Assets each have their own. Hidden everywhere out of the box, because the mistake you cannot take back is a leak.

Check your own work. As the table sees it, beside the Cycle count, redraws the whole board the way a player gets it: masked rows as ???, hidden rows simply absent, numbers gone where you have taken them away, and Help itself switched to what a player reads. Nothing can be changed while you are in it. Press it again to come back.

Some details worth knowing, because they are what a careful GM would go looking for:

  • A Thread with hidden values still shows a bar. The shape of a situation is public even when its arithmetic is not, and a bar is a vague read.
  • A clock with hidden values shows that same bar rather than its segments. Four filled pips out of six is the number, drawn as dots, and counting them is not a workaround.
  • A masked row with a line written instead of the bar shows neither — not the bar, not the pips, and not the contested standings, which are the most precise reading on the board. The sentence stands in for all of it.
  • A masked Thread does not say what kind of Thread it is. There is no mode chip on it, and it draws one plain bar whatever it is really running on: a column of named contenders would say it is being fought over, and counted pips would say something is running out. Every masked Thread on the board is drawn the same way, which is the point.

A screen, not a vault. This hides things from play, not from a determined cheat: Foundry copies world data to every connected client, so a player who goes looking in the developer console can read what is stored. There is no setting anywhere that changes this, in this module or any other: Foundry sends the whole world to every client and leaves permissions to the interface. It is the same bargain every module in this space makes, and it is worth knowing you are making it. As the table sees it proves what a player is SHOWN, which is the part you control; it does not prove what is on their machine.
RSR.help.state.body.player:
Some of this board is deliberately incomplete.

  • A row reading Unknown activity — ???, or anything else ending in ???, is something you know exists but not what it is. What it says in front of the ??? is as much as you have been told.
  • Where one of those would have a bar, you may find a sentence instead. That is what you have heard about it. There is no bar because nobody at the table could tell you how far along it is.
  • Masked rows are all drawn the same way — one plain bar and nothing beside it. You cannot tell from looking whether it is a race between two sides, something counting down, or something being paid for. That is deliberate.
  • A bar with no numbers is something you can see moving without knowing how far it has to go. If another Thread shows counted segments and this one does not, that is the same thing being withheld.
  • And there will be Threads you are not shown at all.

That is the GM keeping the world larger than your current information, which is the whole point of the thing.
RSR.help.tryBody: Builds a complete Plot — two rival Forces, all four Thread modes, a prerequisite chain, committed Assets, and a spread of visibility states. It is real data, so you can edit it, break it and watch the board react. Everything it makes is tagged, and Remove deletes exactly that and nothing you wrote yourself.
RSR.help.removeExampleWarning: Remove every entry the example created? Anything you authored yourself is untouched.
RSR.help.examplePresent: The example is currently in this world.
RSR.settings.defaultVisibility.hint: What players can see about a Plot, Thread, Force or Asset the moment it is created, before you have set its visibility by hand. Hidden is the safe default: nothing you jot down mid-session leaks to the table until you choose to reveal it.
RSR.settings.boardMenu.hint: Opens the Situation Room. The usual way in is the button at the top of the Journal sidebar; this is here in case that sidebar has been customised out from under it.
RSR.notify.noGmForWrite: No Gamemaster is connected, so that change cannot be saved right now.
RSR.notify.relayTimeout: The Gamemaster's client did not confirm that change. Nothing was saved.
RSR.thread.discountHint: Committed Assets have lowered this Thread's cost. The number shown is what it cost before them.
RSR.editor.concludeSummary: Who carried "{name}"? Its threshold is {threshold}. Whoever you pick applies their outcome to the Plot's State.
RSR.editor.reopenHint:
Reactivate this Thread, and take back the State it moved.

What was actually applied is what is reversed, so a change that hit the top or bottom of the range does not invent State on the way back.
RSR.help.advancing.title: Pushing a Thread along
RSR.help.advancing.body.gm:
How a Thread moves depends on its mode, set on the Plot and overridable per Thread.

  • Narrative — tracks nothing. You conclude it when the fiction says so.
  • Investment — one shared pool any Force can pay into. Reaches its threshold on its own.
  • Clock — discrete ticks against a segment count.
  • Contested — every Force keeps its own separate pile.

Moving it. One control, whatever the mode. The dialog asks three things: how far the needle moves, in whose name, and what that does to that Force’s Resources. The cost starts at one per point and is yours to overwrite — a push in nobody’s name is free, because that is you moving the world rather than a Force paying to move it. The note you attach is what the table reads afterwards — and beside it you say how much of the development they read at all.

Concluding. The dialog asks who carried it and shows what each answer would do to State before you commit. Reopen undoes it, reversing exactly what was applied — so a change that hit the top or bottom of the range does not invent State on the way back.

Contested never concludes itself, however far ahead someone is. Who won is a fiction question; the numbers are one input to it, and you are the other.
RSR.help.advancing.body.player:
Threads move in different ways:

  • Some fill up as effort is poured into them.
  • Some tick over in stages.
  • Some are a tug of war between two sides with separate footholds.
  • Some track nothing visible at all, and simply resolve when the story gets there.

Which of those a Thread is doing is usually printed beside its name. A Thread you have not been told about is drawn as a plain bar and nothing else, whichever of them it really is.

When one concludes you will see who carried it and what it did.
RSR.editor.concludeNobodyHint: Concludes the Thread without moving State.
RSR.force.none: No Forces yet. A Plot without anyone pushing it is only weather.
RSR.force.resourcesHint: What this Force has to spend. It is deliberately abstract — coin, favours, sworn swords, whatever the fiction needs it to be this month.
RSR.force.incomeHint:
Paid every Cycle unless you pause this Force.

Income belongs to the Force — what it holds, farms and taxes — not to whether it is currently standing on a Plot.

A negative number is upkeep. It can bankrupt a Force, but never put it in debt.
RSR.force.incomeTooltip: Income per cycle. Struck through means this Force is paused and will draw nothing.
RSR.force.unengaged: On no Plot yet. It still draws its income.
RSR.force.tagsHint:
No mechanical weight. They are there to be read aloud when a Force acts, and to remind you what it should be bad at.

Type one and press + to add it.
RSR.force.adjustHint: GM fiat, for everything the turn clock does not cover: a windfall, a raid, a debt called in. Negative takes it away.
RSR.asset.linkHint:
Optional. Paste a UUID, or drag an Actor, Item or Journal Entry onto this Asset on the board and it fills itself in.

Dragging a document onto a Force creates an Asset from it outright.
RSR.asset.effectHint:
Most Assets are fiction rather than arithmetic, and Does nothing is the honest answer for those.

The other three apply only while this Asset is committed to a Thread: cost reduction lowers that Thread’s threshold, and the other two ride along with every push made into it.
RSR.asset.releaseHint: Take this Asset back into its Force’s hand. Its effect stops applying.
RSR.turn.standing: {label} {turn}. {count} Force(s) will be paid on the next advance.
RSR.turn.advanceSummary: Advance the {label} from {turn} to {next}? Every Force below is listed, including the ones this changes nothing for.
RSR.turn.nobodyPaid: There are no Forces yet, so a cycle passes and nothing moves.
RSR.editor.imageHint: Optional. Browse for an image, or drop an Actor or Journal Entry onto the row on the board and it fills itself in.
RSR.editor.deleteForceWarning: Delete "{name}"? It is removed from {plots} Plot roster(s), from every Thread’s outcomes and standings, and its {assets} Asset(s) are deleted with it. This cannot be undone.
RSR.editor.deleteAssetWarning: Delete "{name}"? Any Thread it was committed to loses its effect. This cannot be undone.
RSR.notify.unresolvedDocument: That document could not be found. Nothing was linked.
RSR.help.forces.title: Forces, Resources and Assets
RSR.help.forces.body.gm:
A Force is a side with its own agenda: an army, a guild, a family, a hunger in the deep. It holds Resources — an abstract currency you define the fiction of — and it spends them to push Threads.

  • Pushing in a Force’s name costs that Force one Resource per point of progress — which is only the figure the push dialog starts at, and yours to overwrite. A push in nobody’s name is free: that is you moving the world, not a Force paying to move it.
  • Income is paid every cycle to every Force, unless you have paused that Force. Where a Force is standing does not change what it earns — a side gathering strength off-screen keeps gathering it.
  • Next Global Cycle sits above the Plot list, beside New Plot, so the world’s clock and the Plots keeping their own are pressed from one screen. It lists every Force before it pays anyone, including the ones it will do nothing for, and names the timers it is about to move, whose Asset each one is and what it is committed to — so an Asset can finish recovering while you are paying wages, and you see it coming. It also names any Plot it will not move, and why: a Plot keeping its own Cycle is advanced from its own button, and one keeping none is never advanced at all. When it is done it says what it moved, because none of what it moves is on the screen you pressed it from. The clock in the header is the Global Cycle; a Plot with its own counts separately, and the two numbers are not meant to agree.

Assets are what a Force can commit: a battalion, a bought magistrate, a dragon who owes nobody anything. Most are pure fiction and carry Does nothing; the rest lower what a Thread costs, or add to every push made into it.

Every Asset also has a condition. Click the badge beside its name to set one: which condition, how long it lasts, and a line about what happened that the table can read.

  • Ready is the normal case and says nothing on the board.
  • Damaged leaves it where it is and halves its effect, rounding down — the original stays on screen with a line through it beside what it is now worth.
  • Suppressed also leaves it where it is, and switches its effect off entirely. Something is holding it down.
  • Inactive takes it off whatever it was committed to and out of the tray, with nothing counting down. You put it back when you decide to.
  • Recovering does the same, and counts down in Cycles. When it reaches zero it becomes Ready on its own and says so in Latest Developments. The number is yours to change or clear at any point.
  • Destroyed asks you to confirm, and files the Asset under Set aside at the bottom of its Force panel.

None of them delete anything: the record, its tags and its history all stay, and every one of them is reversible.

Those six are defaults, not the vocabulary. The table is yours — Settings → Asset conditions. Rename them, change what each one does, delete the ones your campaign has no use for, and add Besieged or Mutinous with whatever switches suit it. Everything above describes what the module ships with; Restore the defaults puts exactly that back, keeping anything you invented. Only Ready cannot be deleted, because it is what an Asset with nothing said about it falls back to.

Drag is the fast path. Open a Plot and its Forces’ uncommitted Assets appear in a tray above the Threads — drag one onto a Thread to commit it, and drag it back onto its Force to release it. Dropping an Actor or Journal Entry onto a Force creates an Asset from it outright.
RSR.help.forces.body.player:
Behind every Plot are Forces — the sides that want something out of it. Each has resources of its own and things it can commit: soldiers, favours, a name that opens doors.

  • When a Force pushes a Thread, something real was spent to move it that far.
  • What a Force spends on one Thread it cannot spend on another.
  • Anything a Force holds may carry a condition beside its name — damaged, driven off, gone. That is the state it is actually in, and it is not decoration: a broken thing helps less, or not at all.
  • A number after the condition is how many Cycles are left before it changes.

Some Forces you will only ever see in outline. Some you will not see at all.
RSR.turn.noTimers: Nothing committed here is on a timer.
RSR.turn.isolatedHint: This Plot keeps its own Cycle. The Global Cycle leaves it alone, and this is the only button that moves it.
RSR.turn.noneHint: This Plot keeps no Cycle at all. Nothing advances it, and there is no button to.
RSR.turn.plotAdvanceHint: Move this Plot’s own Cycle on by one.
RSR.turn.plotAdvancedNotice: {plot}: {label} {turn} began. {arrived} timer(s) arrived. No Resources moved.
RSR.turn.plotNoIncome: No Resources change hands. Income belongs to the Force rather than to any one Plot, and the {label} — still on {turn} — is what pays it.
RSR.force.activeHint: Untick to pause this Force. A paused Force keeps everything it has and is still played normally — it simply stops earning until you resume it.
RSR.force.pauseHint: Pause this Force. It stops drawing income until you resume it.
RSR.force.resumeHint: Resume this Force. It draws income again from the next cycle.
RSR.force.iconHint:
A Font Awesome class for what this Force counts.

fa-solid fa-coins for gold, fa-solid fa-users for levies, fa-solid fa-wheat-awn for grain, fa-solid fa-skull for something worse.
RSR.asset.costNote: Developing this Asset costs {name} {cost} Resource(s), charged when you save it. They hold {resources}.
RSR.asset.dragHint: Drag onto a Thread to commit it. Drag it back here to release it.
RSR.notify.assetUnaffordable: {name} cannot afford that: developing an Asset costs {cost} and they hold {resources}.
RSR.settings.title: Campaign defaults
RSR.settings.forcesNote: What a new Force starts with, and what it costs anyone to develop an Asset.
RSR.settings.forceIconHint:
A Font Awesome class for what a new Force counts.

Each Force can overrule it with its own: coin for one side, levies or grain for another. The preview beside the field is the class you typed, so a typo shows itself before you save.
RSR.settings.assetCostHint:
Charged to the owning Force whenever a new Asset is created — by anyone, including one made by dropping an Actor onto a Force.

Editing an Asset is free. Leave it at zero if Assets in your campaign are earned in the fiction rather than bought.
RSR.settings.plotsNote: What a new Plot or Thread opens with. Changing these never rewrites anything already on the board.
RSR.settings.stateRangeHint:
The span a new Plot’s State bar fills against.

State can be negative if that suits the campaign: “−50 to 50” reads as a situation with two directions, “0 to 100” as one that only builds.
RSR.settings.cycleNote: What the clock the whole board rides is called. This is the one value on this tab that is not a seed: it renames something already on the board rather than the next row you make.
RSR.settings.turnLabelHint:
Leave it empty for Global Cycle.

A campaign counted in something of its own — Moons, Weeks, Marches — says so on the badge in the header, on the confirmation before it advances, and in every line it writes in Latest Developments.

A Plot keeping its own clock names it in its own editor, not here.
RSR.editor.groupHint:
Every Force standing in this Plot, in columns. Drag a chip from one column to another to regroup it, or clear of them all to take it off the Plot.

A heading is purely cosmetic — “The Besiegers”, “The Relief Column”. Nothing reads it to decide anything, and it stops existing when the last Force leaves it.
RSR.editor.pushHint: Advance or pull back this Thread, and say what it cost.
RSR.editor.pushForHint: Move the needle for this Force
RSR.editor.pushAmountHint:
Positive advances, negative pulls back.

The −1 and +1 chips step this number rather than replace it, so a push you are counting out can be pressed rather than typed. Type it instead when you already know it.

A Thread that is already full stays full — the extra is not lost, it simply never happened, and nobody is charged for it.
RSR.editor.pushCostHint:
Negative spends, positive pays out, zero costs nothing.

It starts at one per point moved, which is the usual price. Overwrite it whenever the fiction disagrees: a favour called in is free, and sacking a supply train leaves a Force richer than it started.
RSR.editor.pushNoteHint:
Optional, and public. This is the line the table reads in Latest Developments.

“The dragon swooped in and incinerated the King’s engines.” A number moving is not a development until somebody says what it was.
RSR.notify.contestedNeedsForce: A contested Thread keeps one pile per side, so there is nowhere for a push in nobody’s name to land. Put a Force on this Plot first.
RSR.notify.cannotAfford: {name} cannot spend that — only {resources} in hand.
RSR.log.title: Latest Developments
RSR.log.costHint: What this cost the Force. Only you see this.
RSR.log.clearWarning: Delete every development recorded so far? The board itself is untouched — Plots, Threads, Resources and Assets all stay exactly as they are. Only the account of how they got there is forgotten, and it cannot be brought back.
RSR.help.log.title: Latest Developments
RSR.help.log.body.gm:
Beside the Plot list is the chronicle: every development on the board, newest first. It writes itself. Pushing a Thread, concluding one, committing an Asset, opening a cycle — each leaves a line.

  • The line you actually care about is the note you attach when you move the needle. Everything else is bookkeeping; the note is the fiction.
  • The same dialog asks what the table reads of that development: all of it, the note only, or nothing at all. Decided per push, because the same +1 can be a public rout or a quiet manoeuvre and this is the only moment anyone knows which.
  • What a push cost a Force appears only on your screen.
  • Changing an Asset’s condition writes a line too. Marking the dragon Destroyed is a development, and one the table usually ought to hear about.
  • A development about a masked row keeps its ???. One about a hidden row survives only as its note, with nothing attached to say what it was about — and vanishes entirely if you did not write one.
  • A Plot that keeps its own Cycle writes its own line when you advance it, naming the Plot and the count it has reached. The table reads the same line without the number: that time passed there is theirs to know, and which cycle it was is your bookkeeping.
  • Each line is stamped with the Global Cycle it was written on — including the ones about a Plot keeping its own, since a record kept by two clocks at once is not a record. The line that opens a cycle carries no stamp, because it is the stamp.
  • A line marked Sealed was written while something it names was secret. It stays a note for the table for good.

Revealing a row does not hand the table its past. Names are resolved when a line is read, so hiding a Force takes its name back out of the record — but the seal only ever closes: a development that happened in the dark is still yours to tell in your own words, when you choose to.
RSR.help.log.body.player:
Beside the Plots is a running account of what has been happening, newest first.

  • Some lines name what moved and by how much.
  • Some are just a sentence about something that happened, with no source given. Those are real developments too — you are simply not being told what they touched.
  • Some lines simply mark time passing — for the whole board, or for one Plot that moves at its own pace.
  • Every line is stamped with the cycle it happened on, so you can tell what was recent and what has been sitting there a while.
  • ??? means something is there and you have not been told what it is.
RSR.editor.revertHint: Put every field back to how it was when you opened this editor. What is already saved stays saved.
RSR.editor.discardWarning: You have changes that have not been saved. Leaving now throws them away — the board keeps what it already had.
RSR.editor.hideValuesHint: Hide the numbers without hiding the row. The table still sees this exists and what it is called; they just cannot read how far along it is.
RSR.editor.phaseSeenPlaceholder: Printed under the State bar, for everyone.
RSR.editor.phaseNotesPlaceholder: Yours alone. What you have to remember to do about it.
RSR.editor.removeGroup: Delete this heading. Its Forces stay on the Plot.
RSR.editor.assetsElsewhere: Each of these has its own screen — open one from the chip on this Force’s panel in the Cockpit.
RSR.notify.stateRangeRequired: The maximum has to be above the minimum, or the bar has nothing to fill.
RSR.notify.ownerRequired: An Asset belongs to a Force. Pick one first.
RSR.editor.pushNotePlaceholder: The dragon swooped in and burned the engines.
RSR.help.editing.title: Editing on the board
RSR.help.editing.body.gm:
Every Edit button opens the row where it lives: a Plot from its card or from inside the Plot itself, a Thread inside its Plot, a Force in the Cockpit, an Asset from wherever its chip is. Back returns you to what you were looking at.

  • An editor is the one place on this board that does not save as you type. Nothing reaches the table until you press Save, so a half-written Phase label never appears on anyone’s screen. Revert puts every field back to how it was when you opened it. The notice that follows a save names the row it wrote, so four editors in a row do not blur into one.
  • Phases are cards. Add one, set the State it starts at, name it, pick a tone, and fill in its two texts. They sort by threshold on save, so add them in any order.
  • The roster is columns. Drag a Force between headings to regroup it, drag it clear of every column to take it off the Plot, and use the picker below to add one that is not on it yet. Headings are cosmetic: nothing reads them.
  • A Force’s Assets are listed as chips at the bottom of its editor. Each is a way into that Asset’s own screen, so you do not have to go back out to the Cockpit to reach one.
  • Strengths, weaknesses and prerequisites are chips. Type and press +; press the “✕” to drop one.

Saving writes only the fields the editor owns. A Thread being pushed while you have its editor open keeps that progress — your save will not roll it back.
RSR.help.settings.title: Campaign defaults
RSR.help.settings.body.gm:
The Settings tab holds the numbers you would otherwise retype into every new row: what a Force starts with and earns, what it counts its Resources in, what developing an Asset costs, what a new Thread’s threshold and clock are, and the State range a new Plot opens with.

  • Every field here carries a ⓘ. Hover it for what that number seeds, and what it deliberately does not touch.
  • Cost to develop an Asset is charged to the owning Force when a new Asset is saved — including one made by dropping an Actor onto a Force. Editing an existing Asset is always free.
  • Asset conditions opens the table of states an Asset can be in. Each row says what happens to that Asset’s effect, whether it may still be committed, how many Cycles it lasts and what it becomes afterwards. The six the module ships with are a starting point.
  • The Cycle is what your campaign calls the clock the whole board rides. Leave it empty for Global Cycle. It is the one value on this tab that is not a seed — it renames something already on the board.
  • What the table sees sets the starting visibility for each kind of row separately. Most tables want their Forces named from the start and the Threads those Forces are running kept quiet.

Every value here seeds a new row only. Changing one never reaches back and rewrites a Plot, Thread, Force or Asset that already exists, which is what makes this tab safe to touch mid-campaign.
RSR.editor.pushSeenHint:
What this development looks like in Latest Developments, for everyone but you.

Decided here because the same push can be a public rout or a quiet manoeuvre, and this is the only moment anyone knows which.
RSR.log.seenChipHint:
What the table reads of this line.

Sealed means something it names was secret when it was written, so it stays a note — revealing that row now does not hand the table the past.
RSR.editor.lifecycleHint:
Where this Plot stands as a piece of prep.

  • Active — on the board.
  • Paused — set aside, and still visible.
  • Resolved — finished.
  • Archived — off the board entirely, and the closest thing to deleting it without losing it.
RSR.editor.visibilityHint:
What the table sees of this row.

  • Visible — named, and read in full.
  • Masked — shown to exist as ???, without saying what it is.
  • Hidden — off their screen entirely: not covered up, absent.
RSR.asset.conditionHint:
What state this Asset is in.

A condition can scale its effect down or switch it off, take it off whatever it is committed to, and count down over a number of Cycles before turning into something else.

Which condition does what is yours to set, in Settings.
RSR.asset.conditionNotePlaceholder: Driven off over the river, one wing torn.
RSR.asset.conditionFinalWarning: This one is final: it comes off whatever it is committed to, and it is set aside from what its Force still holds.
RSR.asset.conditionFinalConfirm: Put {name} into {condition}? Nothing is deleted — the record, its tags and its history all stay — but it comes off the board and is set aside from what its Force still holds.
RSR.asset.conditionsSettingsNote: The states an Asset can be in, and what each one does. The six the module ships with are a starting point, not the vocabulary.
RSR.asset.conditionsIntro: Every row is a state an Asset can be put into. Rename them, re-switch them, delete the ones your campaign has no use for, add your own. Ready cannot be deleted: it is what an Asset with nothing said about it resolves to.
RSR.asset.conditionsEffectHint:
What happens to the Asset’s own modifier.

Halved rounds down, so half of a 1-point benefit is nothing — which is the right answer, since rounding it up would make the condition free.
RSR.asset.conditionsInPlayHint: Whether the Asset may be committed. Turning this off takes it off whatever it is on the moment the condition is set, and keeps it out of the tray.
RSR.asset.conditionsCyclesHint:
How long it lasts by default. Zero is no timer at all, which is most of them.

A running timer counts down on the Cycle the Asset is standing on, and you can change or clear it at any point.
RSR.asset.conditionsFinalHint: Ask before setting it, and set the Asset aside from what its Force still holds. Nothing is ever deleted — this is about weight, not data.
RSR.asset.conditionsRestoreHint: Put the six the module ships with back as they were, and keep anything you have added. A built-in you renamed or re-switched is reset.
RSR.asset.rehomeIntro: {count} Asset(s) are in a condition you have deleted. Say what each one becomes — nothing is saved until you do.
RSR.preview.label: As the table sees it
RSR.preview.hint:
Draw the board the way a player gets it: masked rows as ???, hidden rows absent, and numbers withheld wherever you have withheld them.

Nothing can be changed while you are looking.
RSR.preview.banner: You are seeing the board as the table sees it. Anything you are missing is being withheld on purpose.
RSR.editor.maskLabelHint:
What the table sees in place of the name while this is masked.

Leave it empty for the default, which says what kind of thing is being withheld without saying which one.
RSR.editor.maskNotePlaceholder: Rumours about a foreigner running about with a loaded purse, talking to ex-guardsmen.
RSR.editor.maskNoteHintThread: A line the table reads in place of this Thread’s bar, while it is masked. Use it when they have heard something rather than watched it: a bar says how far along it is, and a rumour is not that precise. Leave it empty and the bar stays.
RSR.editor.maskNoteHintPlot: A line the table reads in place of the State bar, while this Plot is masked. Use it when they know a situation is running without being able to read how it is going. Leave it empty and the bar stays.
RSR.settings.forceResourcesHint:
What a new Force is created holding.

A seed and nothing more: changing it never reaches back into a purse already on the board. Use Adjust on the Force itself for that.
RSR.settings.forceIncomeHint:
What a new Force earns each Cycle.

Income belongs to the Force — what it holds, farms and taxes — not to whether it is currently standing on a Plot. A negative number is upkeep, and can bankrupt a Force without ever putting it in debt.
RSR.settings.threadThresholdHint:
What a new Thread has to reach before it concludes itself.

It is read by Investment and Contested Threads. A Clock counts its segments instead, and a Narrative Thread counts nothing — you end that one by hand.
RSR.settings.clockSegmentsHint:
How many segments a new Clock Thread is drawn with.

Six is the familiar one. Four is a scene, eight is a season — the number is the pace, since every tick is the same fraction of it.
RSR.gate.revealed: You locked this; a Phase has opened it.
RSR.graph.none: Nothing on this Plot waits on anything else. Threads gain requirements in their own editor, under Blocked until these conclude.
RSR.graph.unknownHint:
This Thread waits on one you cannot see.

You are told that it is waiting, and not for what: naming it, or even drawing an arrow from where it would have stood, would give it away.
RSR.graph.tangled: These wait on each other and can never open:
RSR.editor.statusHint:
Locked is your own switch: the Thread is on the board and cannot be pushed or concluded.

It is not the only thing that shuts a Thread. A requirement that has not concluded shuts it too, and so does a Phase this Plot has reached — and a Phase that reveals this Thread opens it again over the top of this switch.

Concluded is set by concluding it, not here.
RSR.graph.orphans: {count} other Thread(s) here require nothing and are required by nothing.
RSR.help.gating.title: Gates and requirements
RSR.help.gating.body.gm:
A Thread can be shut in three ways, and they are independent — any one of them is enough on its own.

  • Locked — your own switch, in the Thread’s editor. You have decided it is not available.
  • A requirement — a Thread named under Blocked until these conclude that has not concluded yet.
  • A Phase — the Plot has climbed to a Phase whose card names this Thread under Locks.

A Phase’s Reveals list is the counterpart: it opens a Thread you had locked, and the row says so. It does not pay off a requirement — revealing a Thread that still waits on another leaves it waiting, or you would silently be skipping the chain you built in front of it.

  • A shut Thread cannot be pushed or concluded, by you either. The way through is to open the gate: throw the switch, conclude what it is waiting on, or move State off the Phase that shut it.
  • Committing an Asset to a shut Thread is still allowed. Standing a battalion by ahead of a door opening is exactly what a gate you can see is for.
  • A Thread cannot be made to require one that already waits on it, at any depth — the picker does not offer it, because two Threads waiting on each other would never open.

Requirements, beside Threads in an open Plot, draws what waits on what: a column per step, arrows pointing the way the work has to go. Only Threads that are part of a requirement are drawn — the rest are counted underneath, because cards with no arrow on them bury the ones that have them.

Nothing about a gate is stored. It is worked out from where State stands now, so typing State back under a Phase reopens what that Phase shut. A gate answers whether a Thread is available, not what once happened to it — which is why it can never go stale, and why it can change under you when a conclusion moves the bar.
RSR.help.gating.body.player:
Not every Thread on a Plot is open. Some are waiting on something.

  • A Thread that is not open yet says so, and it has no controls on it.
  • If what it is waiting on is a Thread you can see, it is named. If it is not, you are told only that something has to happen first — never what.
  • Requirements, beside Threads, draws the ones that wait on each other. A card marked and something else is waiting on a Thread you have not been shown.

And a Thread being shut is not always about another Thread. The situation itself can close things off as it worsens, and open them again when it eases.
